newsitem.title: USA: Massachusetts grapples with capital programs.
newsitem.headline: Massachusetts grapples with capital programs.

text.p: Budget battles in the 1997-98 biennial legislative session into clearer focus as House and Senate conferees try to sort out their differences this week so that at least some capital projects can proceed.

The measure authorizing $685 million in bonds to upgrade the state's court facilities over the next several years, which was passed by both houses, but sent back by Gov. William Weld with an amendment, has languished awaiting action.

Weld wants the lawmakers to strike from the bill language requiring that union-only labor be used on courthouse projects. Weld argues that in the western part of the state, local workers who are not members of labor unions would be precluded from construction jobs.
House Speaker Thomas Finneran said last week he and members of his leadership are considering some modification of the union provision.

Meanwhile, there appears to be some movement on a convention center for Boston. Finneran, who had objected to any state financing without a new revenue source for the proposed $700 million center, appears to have mellowed.

He says he now expects the House will pass a bill laying out a funding plan for the center in South Boston by the time lawmakers take a summer break in July in part because of a measure proposed by the governor.

Weld is set to appear before the State Administration Committee Monday to urge passage of the bill that would provide the bulk of the state's share of the convention center financing by way of a 2.3 percent hike in hotel room occupany tax in Boston and Cambridge. Voters, however, would still have to approve the measure in a referendum.

And the House Committee on Long-Term Debt is still struggling to identify how much the state is in debt, for what purposes and how the red ink can be erased. Lawmakers have authorized $21 billion in borrowing - much more than Wall Street says is prudent.
After receiving testimony from legislators and other state officials, the committee is expected to issue a report on how the state should manage its debt.
Massachusetts has a $900 million-a-year cap on the amount that can be borrowed for capital improvements.

Right now, legislators claim victory when they get a bill passed authorizing borrowing for a project, but the administration can wait as long as it wants to actually do the borrowing. That means projects wait for years while the state sink deeper into the hole.
